The Moon is 50.95 percent illuminated, 90.942 degrees from the Sun, and 401155.2 kilometers away. Yes—**you’d probably be able to spot the Moon**, though it may take some deliberate searching.

- It is **12.2° above the horizon**, toward **azimuth 114°**—roughly east-southeast. Make sure that part of the horizon is unobstructed.
- At **50.95% illumination** and **90.9° from the Sun**, it is approximately a **first-quarter/near-quarter Moon**, which is bright enough to be visible in daylight.
- The Sun is high and the sky is bright, so the Moon will have relatively low contrast. Its modest altitude also means haze, buildings, trees, and atmospheric scattering could make it harder.
- With clear skies and an unobstructed view, an ordinary observer who knows the direction should generally find it with unaided vision.

Look about **12° above the east-southeastern horizon**—roughly 1–2 fist widths at arm’s length above the horizon, depending on your hand measurement. Avoid looking anywhere near the Sun; use the stated azimuth and keep the Sun well out of your field of view.
